scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The galop originated in southwestern Germany as the 'Hopser' or 'Rutscher' before being introduced to Paris in the late 1820s by the Duchesse de Berry.
It gained immense popularity in Vienna, Berlin, and London throughout the 19th century, often serving as the final dance of a ball.
on_screen: Map: France, Germany, Austria · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The galop was frequently used as the 'Kehraus' or final dance of the evening at balls, signaling the conclusion of the event.
It is also associated with hunt balls and wedding receptions.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Danced in a closed position, the galop consists of rapid, lateral sliding steps (chassés) performed in a 2/4 time signature.
Dancers move with a springing, light motion, often traveling in circles or across the room.
The dance is characterized by its high tempo and the 'galop step', which involves a slide and a closing of the feet.
Watch for Galop step.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (NZaeTPXlKAg)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Circular or linear movement around the ballroom.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is written in a fast 2/4 meter.
Historically, it was played by ballroom orchestras featuring strings, brass, and woodwinds.
Listen for the Orchestral strings, Brass (specifically cornet), Woodwinds.
The pulse is 2/4.
A driving, high-tempo orchestral sound characterized by a crisp, rhythmic pulse that mimics the rapid, galloping movement of a horse.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: In the 1820s, the dance prompted a shift in women's fashion, with dresses shortened to the ankle to allow for the rapid, sliding footwork.
It was primarily a ballroom dance, performed in formal social settings.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The Duchesse de Berry is credited with introducing the dance to Paris.
Composers including Johann Strauss II, Franz Liszt, Hans Christian Lumbye, and Dmitri Shostakovich wrote numerous galops.
In Australia, the dance is known as 'galopede'.
The galop is a precursor to the polka and influenced the development of the can-can.

scenes.title: Family tree
